title: Threads, data races and lifetime

objectives.text: Identify potentially concurrent conflicting non-atomic accesses lacking happens-before, separating a sequential lost-update model from undefined C++ data races.
Keep worker inputs/results alive through completion and use scoped C++20 joining with disjoint result ownership rather than sleeps, detach or premature reads.

blocks.markdown: Threads in one process share its address space, not an automatic correctness protocol. Each thread has its own execution state, but a captured reference can designate an object another thread also uses. Concurrency means work can overlap in lifetime; it need not run simultaneously on distinct CPU cores. Scheduler order, sleeps and a test that happened to pass do not establish a C++ synchronization relationship. Before starting workers, list every shared input/output, who reads/writes it, its lifetime and the event ordering that makes those accesses safe.

Under C++ rules, two evaluations conflict when one modifies a memory location (or starts/ends an overlapping object lifetime) and the other reads/modifies the relevant location or starts/ends an overlapping lifetime. Potentially concurrent conflicting actions, at least one non-atomic, with neither happening before the other constitute a data race, subject to the standard signal-handler exception outside this lesson. Such a C++ data race is undefined behavior. Two reads of unchanged valid data do not by themselves conflict. Different ordinary array elements can be different memory locations; that is not a license to mutate the container structure concurrently, and packed specializations such as vector<bool> need separate care.

To reason about a logical lost update, split an abstract increment into read old value, then write old+1. Start counter=0; A-read0, B-read0, A-write1, B-write1 ends at 1 instead of 2 in this declared sequential model. The code below executes those model events in ONE Python thread. It is not a sample of racy C++ behavior and does not enumerate all possible outcomes of undefined behavior. Do not run unsynchronized non-atomic C++ increments and claim the only risk is losing one update.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: AABB 2; ABAB 1; ABBA 1; BAAB 1; BABA 1; BBAA 2. These are all six order-preserving schedules of two modeled read/write pairs. This small sequential model demonstrates a logical read-modify-write gap only. It is neither a weak-memory model nor a dynamic C++ race detector.

blocks.markdown: A simpler concurrent design can eliminate shared mutation: immutable values are read by both workers, each worker writes exactly one distinct ordinary long long result element, and main reads results only AFTER both workers finish and joining completes. Creating the initialized inputs before starting the workers and successful joining provide the needed publication/completion ordering. The input and result objects are declared before an inner scope holding the worker handles, so they outlive every normal join. No vector resizing, aliasing overlapping outputs or main-thread early result read is allowed.

blocks.caption: C++20, compile/link with -pthread and warnings. Expected output: 6 15, then 21. No worker prints, so output order is deterministic despite unknown worker execution order. Two bounded 3-element sums use safe long long arithmetic on fixed small int inputs. This demonstrates race-free ownership/joining, NOT a speedup or production parallel reduction. C++ app runner remains unverified.

blocks.markdown: Destruction is reverse construction order: second then first jthread join inside the inner scope, then main reads partial, and only later partial/values are destroyed. A still-joinable jthread destructor requests stop and joins; stop is cooperative, not forced termination. These lambdas ignore stop but finish bounded nonblocking work, so a stop request is not needed for their completion. If second-thread construction fails, the already constructed first handle is unwound and joins before referents leave scope. This is a source-contract argument, not injected thread-creation failure evidence. This example has no throwing worker operation; an uncaught exception escaping a thread entry invokes terminate rather than propagating to the parent like a normal function call.

A successful join orders that worker completion before the joining thread continues, but it does not retroactively repair a race that happened earlier between two workers. Joining both unsafely incrementing workers at the end is still wrong. std::thread destruction while joinable calls terminate; jthread provides scoped stop/join behavior, but detaching loses its lifetime protection. Never detach a worker borrowing a local that can disappear. A joining destructor can block forever if the worker waits forever, ignores necessary stop requests or deadlocks; ownership safety is not a deadline guarantee.

To investigate a race, record both accesses, source locations, threads, object ownership/lifetime and missing happens-before path. A ThreadSanitizer report gives dynamic evidence about instrumented executed paths; a clean run cannot prove all schedules or unexecuted code safe. Instrumented testing changes time/memory behavior and has platform/toolchain constraints; do not publish its latency as an uninstrumented production benchmark. AddressSanitizer/UBSan alone are not data-race detectors. No intentionally racy native program is run in this lesson. Next synchronization lesson introduces mutexes/atomics and why a logically incorrect protocol can remain data-race-free.

Independent transfer: give each worker a separate result slot, keep input immutable, aggregate only after joining and compare with a sequential reference for empty and uneven partitions. State which properties rely on object declaration order and which rely on join. Review a hypothetical capture-by-reference worker that escapes its owner, without executing undefined behavior. Explain why sleep(1), volatile and a million passing repetitions do not replace ownership and specified synchronization.

Sources: [C++ data races](https://eel.is/c++draft/intro.races), [jthread](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/jthread.html), [successful join synchronization](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/thread/join.html), and [ThreadSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSanitizer.html). The live draft and reference pages include post-C++20 material; this source uses only C++20 jthread/ordinary arrays/join lifetime, not later thread attributes or a full weak-memory formalization.

summary: Race review needs object identity, access kind, lifetime and specified ordering. A sequential lost-update model is not permission to execute C++ undefined behavior. Immutable inputs, disjoint ordinary result slots and scoped joining can avoid shared mutation; clean tests and sleeps do not prove race freedom.
